title: Why will people use this offer?
rows: 1. Do customers share the same basic objectives?
What are the objectives in using this product or service, and how do customer types differ? Keep this high-level; the customer-objectives worksheet explores the differences in more detail.
2. What reasons justify choosing you over a competitor?
Identify the rationales that should be communicated clearly through the experience. Defining them at the outset helps make design choices consistent.
3. What must the offering accomplish for the business?
Write clear success criteria that can guide decisions rather than leave success undefined.
4. If the offer is the answer, what is the question?
Describe the customer problem concisely. Formulating the business proposition as an answer helps clarify what it is really about.
note: Use the accessible text as the main reading. Source scans remain optional supporting material.

context.label: When to use it
context.text: At the start of a project, whether the offering already exists or is new.

context.label: Purpose
context.text: Start with a clear proposition: customer wants, business objectives and reasons to choose this offer. Writing answers can expose differences in the team’s understanding.

context.label: Ready to move on when
context.text: The team agrees on the proposition, believes it has a viable market position and can explain why customers would choose it.

title: Align the experience with customer identity
rows: 1. What does choosing the offer say about the customer?
Treat the brand, product or service as an avatar: what values or beliefs is the customer communicating?
2. Who is the customer telling that story to?
Consider themselves, colleagues, peers, friends or a wider audience.
3. Does it express membership of a group or community?
Identify any relevant social belonging rather than assuming all customers share one identity.
4. How important is expressing individuality?
Consider how much the intended customer wants to emphasize their individual identity.
note: Use the accessible text as the main reading. Source scans remain optional supporting material.

context.text: After clarifying why people will use the offer; keep that proposition available.

context.label: Ready to move on when
context.text: You understand the customer’s self-image and how the offer reflects it. Record implementation ideas alongside each question.

title: Understand what customers want to achieve
rows: 1. Objectives
What does the customer want to achieve from the product, service or experience? Try the wording “I want to…”.
2. Subtext
What is the difference between what people say and what they mean? Record possible unspoken desires or issues, distinguishing research evidence from your assumptions.
3. Deeper objectives

Ask why the stated objective matters, then continue asking why until the higher goal becomes clear. The source example distinguishes taking a photo from sharing experiences with friends/family or expressing creativity. The repeated “I want to / Why?” writing spaces support tracing more than one objective.
4. Business objectives
What are the business goals for this particular customer type?
5. Notes and ideas
Capture ideas suggested by a better understanding of customer objectives.
note: Use the accessible text as the main reading. Source scans remain optional supporting material.

context.label: When to use it
context.text: After the proposition and brand-appeal worksheets. Complete a separate record for each customer type and revise it as research reveals differences.

context.label: Purpose
context.text: Identify distinct customer profiles and the higher objectives they seek from the offering.

context.label: Ready to move on when
context.text: You understand the customer types the experience must satisfy and what each wants to achieve.

title: Map where the customer experience starts and ends
rows: Stages in this customer’s journey
List the stages in a scenario. The source holiday example starts with deciding to go on holiday, followed by deciding where to go.
Principles relevant to each stage

Consider customer identity, objectives, expectations, effort, stress, sensory pleasure, social pleasure, customer control and emotions. These are the nine legend labels visible on the supplied sheet; do not infer an additional supplied worksheet.
Example links between a stage and principles
The example links deciding to go on holiday with effort, stress and control, and choosing where to go with objectives, effort, stress from excess choice and sensory pleasure.

context.label: When to use it
context.text: After the proposition, brand identity and customer-objectives work.

context.label: Purpose
context.text: Explore the complete end-to-end journey and opportunities outside obvious purchase/use moments. Stages need not occur in one fixed order; use more than one record if needed.

context.label: Ready to move on when
context.text: You cannot trace an earlier beginning or later ending, and you have identified the high-level stages and relevant experience principles. Revisit the map when you discover omissions.

title: Break a journey stage into tasks and touchpoints
rows: Success criteria
Record customer and business objectives for this stage separately; each supplies its own definition of success.
Preconditions
What must the customer already have done before they can start and successfully complete this stage?
Steps, touchpoints and relevant principles
For each required step, identify the touchpoint—such as cellphone, website, shop or call centre—and the principles to review. Steps may occur in different orders.
Supplied example
A search for “cheap flights” uses a search engine; viewing flight options uses a travel-comparison site. The example marks effort as a relevant principle for both.
Principle legend
Identity, objectives, expectations, effortlessness, stress, sensory pleasure, social pleasure, control and emotions are the visible legend labels.
note: Use the accessible text as the main reading. Source scans remain optional supporting material.

context.label: When to use it
context.text: After the customer-objectives and end-to-end journey sheets. It can also be a starting point for improving a small part of an existing experience.

context.label: Purpose
context.text: Break a stage into smaller tasks so that each step, touchpoint and possible improvement can be examined. Use a separate record for each stage and revise it as research progresses.

context.label: Ready to move on when
context.text: You have identified the smaller tasks, available touchpoints and the experience principles to improve for each.

title: Connect customer emotions with triggers and responses
rows: Possible negative emotions
Anger; annoyance; anxiety; apprehension; boredom; disappointment; disgust; distraction; doubt; embarrassment; frustration; neglect; regret; shock. Add others relevant to the stage.
Possible positive emotions
Acceptance; admiration; amazement; anticipation; calmness; delight; excitement; interest; joy; pride; relaxation; satisfaction; surprise; trust. These are prompts, not a diagnostic taxonomy.
Emotions to promote
For each intended emotion, identify the trigger and what the business could do appropriately.
Emotions to avoid
For each unwanted emotion, identify the likely trigger and a prevention or response strategy.
Working columns
Record the emotion, its trigger and the strategy. Distinguish an observed customer response from an assumption about what someone feels.

title: The CEO operating review: 15 areas of responsibility
rows: Vision and strategy

Develop a clear company vision with input from the CFO and other senior leaders. Align financial goals with strategic objectives and include financial perspectives in sustainable growth planning. Review the strategy against performance, align understanding across the company, examine industry changes and communicate the direction to stakeholders.
Leadership and culture

Encourage collaboration across departments, recognize performance and work with the CFO on financial ethical standards. Support creativity and innovation, prioritize customer needs in strategic planning, communicate openly and champion collaborative team-building. The second innovation encouragement in this column is consolidated into this item.
Financial management

Work with the finance function on financial health, budgeting and cash flow. Review capital expenditure, investment and risk decisions. Develop reporting and audit processes, review performance against targets and adjust plans. Examine cost efficiency and compliance with applicable financial/reporting requirements.
Corporate governance

Work with the CFO and relevant leaders on governance, accurate reporting, compliance, controls and fraud prevention. Check alignment with mission and values, transparency, company policies and corporate legal responsibilities. Encourage ethical conduct.
Risk management

Identify financial and operational exposures with the finance function and other owners, then agree appropriate responses. Monitor exposure and events, maintain a risk framework, review procedures, include risk in decisions and communicate relevant practices to stakeholders.
Operational efficiency

The source repeats risk identification here; it is retained once in the risk-management area above. Improve productive systems and processes, monitor operational performance and plan improvements. Encourage continuous improvement and evaluate useful technology. Review supply-chain management and resolve operational issues promptly.
Talent management

Work with HR, finance and other owners on talent strategy. Support development, career progression and effective performance-management systems. Plan succession, balance skills and experience, and support a culture of learning and professional development.
Customer focus

Review satisfaction, customer-centred practices and the financial viability of products/services with finance and marketing. Gather and analyze feedback, check that the offer meets needs, maintain customer relationships and engage directly with customers to understand concerns.
Investor relations

Coordinate with the CFO on clear communication with investors and analysts. Build appropriate relationships with current and potential investors. Report performance and prospects consistently, respond to questions and maintain transparency.
Brand reputation

Represent the company in relevant public forums and maintain constructive media relationships. Develop a clear narrative, align actions with the brand image, manage reputation risks and engage stakeholders.
Innovation and technology

Support innovation, stay informed about relevant technologies and oversee implementation. Encourage cross-functional creative problem-solving. Review R&D investment and digital-transformation initiatives, and anticipate technological disruption.
Sustainability and CSR

Connect CSR strategy to business objectives and oversee sustainability practices. Monitor and report performance, engage stakeholders and bring sustainability concerns to the board. Review strategy, support employee learning and consider sustainable/ethical practices across the supply chain.
Stakeholder management

Identify relevant stakeholders and prioritize engagement with regard to influence and interest. Build constructive relationships, take responsibility for stakeholder impacts, examine value creation and listen to concerns. Provide communication and feedback routes, maintain appropriate transparency, manage conflicts and report relevant company performance.
Mergers and acquisitions

Connect M&A strategy to business objectives. Oversee diligence, negotiation, legal requirements and early financing planning. Review strategic fit and realistic synergy assumptions. Plan integration and communicate the transaction’s purpose and progress. Address culture integration and monitor delivery against financial objectives and expected synergies.
Continuity and succession

Maintain and review business-continuity arrangements for a crisis and succession plans for executive roles. Develop internal talent, communicate relevant plans and prepare successors. Check critical-role coverage and support organizational resilience and adaptability.
